[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="15" screen_mobile_spacer_size="10"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. As a public art sculptor, I design large-scale work for the places people walk through — foyers, plazas, precincts, gardens and festival sites. Three strands: kinetic sculpture that moves, figurative sculpture with volume and character, and architectural sculpture at landmark scale.[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text]The work starts as a 3D model and ends with something installed and lit. In 2019 that meant a 2.1-metre carved baobab on stage at Signal, a City of Melbourne venue — designed here, carved from polystyrene by a Victorian fabricator, reinforced, lit and projection-mapped. Related practices often end up in the same commission: installation art, projection and topiary.[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]What Is Kinetic Sculpture?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Kinetic sculpture is sculpture with parts that move. The movement can come from wind, water, a motor, or a programmed trigger, and it belongs to the artwork rather than being decoration bolted on. A static sculpture is resolved from every angle at once. A kinetic one changes while you stand in front of it.

It is a young form compared with carving or casting, so there is still a lot of unclaimed ground in it. That is most of the appeal.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]What Oddtoe adds is the trigger. Movement can be started by a sensor, a robot, or a piece of code — a system of triggers, actions and interactions, closer to a Rube Goldberg drawing than a motor on a timer. George Rhoads planned his kinetic systems that way, on paper, before anything was built.

Kinetic work rarely stands alone here. It usually arrives as the moving element inside a larger piece — a planted topiary setting, an installation, or a robotic figure.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="Three strands, one workshop" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]What Kinds of Sculpture Does Oddtoe Make?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Kinetic, figurative, and architectural. They share a process — designed in 3D, fabricated in real material, finished, lit and installed — and they suit different briefs. A fourth strand, inflatable sculpture, gets its scale from air instead of material.

Kinetic. Moving work for foyers, festivals and venues where the piece needs to do something, not just sit there.

Figurative. Volume and character. Faces, creatures, bodies with too much of themselves. General with Pinkeye, a portrait bust designed in 2024, is where this one lives — modelled and resolved in 3D, waiting on a stone commission to be carved.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Architectural. The big end — landmark and gateway pieces where the sculpture has to be engineered as much as designed. Footings, loads, wind, sign-off. This is the strand a developer or council is usually shopping for.

Most commissions borrow from more than one. The baobab was architectural in scale and fabrication, figurative in shape, and it moved — with projection rather than motors.

Related pages: robotics, props and fabrication, sensory gardens.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="Which one does your site need?" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Kinetic, Figurative, or Architectural Sculpture?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/6"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="2/3"][vc_column_text css=""]The three strands answer different briefs. This table sets out where each one goes, what it is made from, what the site has to provide, and what Oddtoe hands over.

  Kinetic Figurative Architectural
What it is Sculpture with parts that move A figure, face or creature Structural work built into a site
Where it goes Foyers, atriums, festivals Plazas, retail, hospitality, gardens Gateways, precincts, building forecourts
Typical materials Metal, composites, bearings, motors Carved foam, resin, composite finishes Steel, stone, engineered foam, composites
Site requirements Power and clearance for movement A footing or plinth Engineering sign-off, footings, rigging
Ongoing upkeep Moving parts serviced periodically Surface cleaning and repair Structural inspection
What Oddtoe delivers Concept, 3D design, mechanism, install Concept, 3D design, fabrication, finish Concept, 3D design, fabrication drawings, install

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/6"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="who" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="Councils, developers, architects, and private collectors" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Who Commissions Large-Scale Sculpture in Australia?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Councils, property developers, architects, festivals and venues — and increasingly it is a planning requirement rather than a preference. Australian councils run "percent for art" schemes that oblige a development to spend a share of its construction budget on public art.

In Western Australia the state Percent for Art Scheme sets that at up to one per cent of the construction budget for new works over $2 million. Other councils set their own rates and thresholds, and some accept a cash contribution instead of a physical work.

The practical effect: your buyer often has a number attached before the brief is written.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Developers and architects commission the piece that gives a building its forecourt moment and satisfies the public art condition at the same time.

Councils and precincts commission work that pulls people into a laneway, park or main street, and that survives a decade of weather and hands.

Festivals and venues commission for a season — built fast, installed on a bump-in schedule, struck at the end. Oddtoe has done exactly this at a City of Melbourne venue.

Private collectors and families commission a single piece for a garden, courtyard or entrance, usually figurative and usually personal.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="built" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="A 2.1-metre carved baobab at a City of Melbourne venue" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]What Does an Oddtoe Commission Look Like?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]A 2.1-metre baobab tree, designed in 3D, carved from polystyrene, reinforced, lit from within, projection-mapped, and installed at Signal for the Melbourne International Comedy Festival in 2019. It was the centrepiece of Babbling with Baobabs, Oddtoe's own children's show, staged across two performances on 1 and 2 April.

Design. Built as an electronic 3D model here in the studio, with the branch geometry limited to sections thick enough to survive a carve and a load-in.

Fabrication. Carved from medium-density expanded polystyrene by Industrial Carving Services in Kilsyth, Victoria, from that model, and delivered raw on an MDF base.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Finishing. Branches strengthened with epoxy resin and fibreglass cloth, then the whole form coated with timber flakes to give it bark.

Light and projection. LED lighting inside the trunk, diffused and undiffused, plus animation projection-mapped onto the surface and run live from Resolume — grass climbing the trunk, weather moving across it, a glowing hollow where the tree's face appeared.

Voice. A "Baobab Translator" prototyped on Amazon Alexa let the audience talk to the tree and get an answer back. It is the working ancestor of the talking-plant idea described on the installation art page.

Install. Bump-in, rigging and lighting plot in a single morning, on a council venue's schedule.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="how" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="From expression of interest to install day" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]How Does a Sculpture Commission Work?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Six steps: the brief and the site, concept and 3D model, engineering and materials, fabrication, finish and lighting, then installation. Public commissions usually open with an EOI — a short proposal, a CV and images of relevant work — before any design is paid for.

1. Brief and site. Dimensions, access, footings, power, sightlines, weather exposure and how long the piece has to last.

2. Concept and 3D model. Designed in 3D so the commissioner sees the piece in the actual space before anything is cut.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]3. Engineering and materials. What it is made of, how it is fixed down, and what a structural engineer needs to sign.

4. Fabrication. Carving, casting or building, with specialist fabricators where the scale calls for it, and regular progress updates rather than a long silence.

5. Finish and lighting. Surface, coating, weatherproofing, and light — which is what decides whether the piece exists after dark.

6. Installation. On site, on the agreed day, to the venue or builder's programme.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="default_row_small_paddings" anchor="humour" dfd_row_responsive_enable="dfd-row-responsive-enable" responsive_styles="padding_left_mobile:10|padding_right_mobile:10"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="50" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_family:BebasNeueRegular|letter_spacing:0" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_family:QwigleyRegular" subtitle="The Botero argument" heading_margin="margin-bottom:10px;"]Why Humour in Public Sculpture?[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]Because most public art is solemn, and the popular exceptions usually are not. Fernando Botero put voluminous bronze figures into plazas from Medellín to the Champs-Élysées to Singapore, and people queue to photograph them. Critics describe the work as monumental exaggeration carrying humour and social criticism at the same time.

That is the tradition Oddtoe works in — not the scale of it, the intent. Volume, character, and a piece that is pleased to see you.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4" css=".vc_custom_oddtoe_col_gutter{padding-left: 20px;padding-right: 20px;}"][vc_column_text css=""]For a commissioner the argument is not sentimental. A sculpture people photograph is a sculpture that travels: onto phones, into feeds, into the local paper. A solemn abstract form in a forecourt does a quieter job.

It also ages differently. Work made to be liked tends to be defended by the people who live near it, which matters when a council reviews a collection.

Oddtoe's figurative work sits here — General with Pinkeye and the portrait bust series, all volume and attitude, currently designed and resolved in 3D rather than carved. A commission is what takes one of them into stone at scale. More of that thinking on the weird art page.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay=""][vc_column width="1/4"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/2"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="120" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="100" screen_tablet_spacer_size="80" screen_mobile_spacer_size="80"][vc_column_text item_animation="transition.fadeIn"]

Questions about

Commissioning sculpture?

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="30" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][dfd_accordion style="style-3" active_section="1" font_size="18" tab_title_google_fonts="yes" tab_title_custom_fonts="font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal" icon_size="14"][vc_tta_section title="What does a public art sculptor do?" tab_id="1755400000001-public-art-sculptor-faq-1"][vc_column_text css=""]

A public art sculptor designs and delivers sculpture for places the public moves through — plazas, foyers, parks, precincts and festival sites. The work covers the concept, the 3D design, the engineering and fabrication, the finish, and the installation on site. Oddtoe works across kinetic, figurative and architectural sculpture.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What is kinetic sculpture?" tab_id="1755400000002-public-art-sculptor-faq-2"][vc_column_text css=""]

Kinetic sculpture is sculpture with parts that move. The movement can come from wind, water, motors, or a programmed trigger, and it is part of the artwork rather than decoration added to it. A static sculpture is resolved from every angle at once; a kinetic one changes while you stand in front of it.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="How much does a large-scale sculpture commission cost?" tab_id="1755400000003-public-art-sculptor-faq-3"][vc_column_text css=""]

Cost is driven by scale, materials, how much engineering and certification the site needs, fabrication, transport and installation. A single indoor figure and an engineered outdoor landmark are very different budgets. Oddtoe quotes each brief individually — send the site, the dates and the budget range.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="How long does a sculpture commission take?" tab_id="1755400000004-public-art-sculptor-faq-4"][vc_column_text css=""]

As a worked example: the 2.1-metre baobab for Babbling with Baobabs went from concept in January 2019 to carved delivery in mid-March and onto the stage at Signal on 1 April — about three months, concept to install. Larger outdoor commissions needing engineering sign-off and council approvals run longer.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What materials do you work in?" tab_id="1755400000005-public-art-sculptor-faq-5"][vc_column_text css=""]

Carved polystyrene and engineered foam, metal, stone, resin and composites, plus living material where a piece sits in a garden. The baobab was carved from medium-density expanded polystyrene, then reinforced with epoxy resin and fibreglass cloth and coated with timber flakes.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Can Oddtoe handle fabrication and installation, or design only?" tab_id="1755400000006-public-art-sculptor-faq-6"][vc_column_text css=""]

Both. Oddtoe designs in 3D, then works with specialist fabricators and installs on site. The baobab was carved by Industrial Carving Services in Kilsyth, Victoria, from Oddtoe's own 3D model, then finished, lit and installed by the studio.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Where is Oddtoe based, and where do you install?" tab_id="1755400000007-public-art-sculptor-faq-7"][vc_column_text css=""]

Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia, and works with clients in Los Angeles and Berlin. Sculpture is delivered in Melbourne and across Australia, with travel quoted up front for interstate and overseas sites.
